name: Central Michigan Buffer Zone: A Freight Broker's Regional Guide
author: Oskar Dembele-Magnusson, Dembele-Magnusson Transit Consulting
description: A freight broker's practical field guide to navigating the Central Michigan buffer zone between GLMZ and Detroit, including routes, communities, trade goods, and hazards.
body:
CENTRAL MICHIGAN BUFFER ZONE — REGIONAL ASSESSMENT
Prepared for: New Courier Intake, Tier 2 Freight Certification
Author: Dembele-Magnusson Transit Consulting, East Corridor Division

The Central Michigan buffer zone is not nothing. I want to be clear about this before you get the wrong idea and either underprepare or overprepare. It is not wilderness. It is not a dead zone. It is a place where about four hundred thousand people have been living for two hundred years without asking GLMZ or Detroit for permission, and they have opinions about couriers who treat them like backdrop.

GEOGRAPHY AND DISTANCE
Figure roughly 280 kilometers east from the GLMZ outer freight ring to the Detroit Compact border. The old I-96 corridor is the spine — maintained, more or less, by the Corridor Communities Collective, which assesses a passage toll at checkpoints near Howell, Brighton, and Fowlerville. The toll is reasonable. Pay it. The CCC has road crews and they do good work. The alternative routes through the county roads are faster in good weather and catastrophic in bad, and Central Michigan has bad weather seven months of the year.

COMMUNITIES AND WHAT THEY TRADE
Howell Junction is the largest settlement, maybe twelve thousand people in the metro area. It functions as a trade hub between the two megacities and has elevated itself accordingly — banking services in Φ and in Detroit scrip, a medical clinic with actual trained staff, two competing freight exchanges, and a black market for GLMZ-restricted goods that everyone knows about and no one discusses. If you're picking up or dropping off anything that needs to clear customs at either end, the brokers in Howell will have opinions about the paperwork.

Fowlerville grew up around a water processing facility that still works. Clean water is their primary export. They are specific about payment and will not negotiate on price. This is non-optional — they have the water and you need it. They are otherwise pleasant.

The communities east of Howell get smaller and stranger in roughly equal measure. Brighton Township maintains a wall — not hostile, they'll trade, but you approach the main gate and you wait to be acknowledged before you proceed. They lost people to a misunderstanding in 2197 and they have not forgotten it. If you are asked to state your business, state it plainly and do not embellish.

Salem was a dairy community that retooled into hydroponic protein cultivation after the bovine respiratory epidemics of 2189-2191. They grow a dense, calorie-rich grain substitute that GLMZ food processors pay well for. The smell is difficult to describe. You adapt.

HAZARDS, PRACTICAL
Animal predation is real. The large mammal population in the buffer zone has recovered aggressively over two hundred years of low human density, and the apex predators do not distinguish between wildlife and freight drivers. Keep your vehicle sealed at night. The communities along the corridor know this and will tell you which stretches have active wolf or bear presence if you ask.

Route variance is the biggest logistical issue. Roads that are passable in September may be impassable in March. The CCC maintains a radio network that broadcasts daily route conditions — tune to 88.7 on the analog band, not the digital overlay, which is unreliable east of Howell. If a community radio says a road is closed, the road is closed and the community has a reason.

HAZARDS, LESS PRACTICAL
I am including this section because I have had three couriers file incident reports in the last eighteen months describing what they call 'road confusion' — arriving at a known intersection and finding the geometry wrong, roads meeting at angles inconsistent with the maps, landmarks in the wrong position. I do not have an explanation for this. I have had the maps checked. The maps are correct. I have had the couriers checked. They are sober. My current working theory is GPS drift compounded by fatigue and unfamiliar terrain. This theory does not fully satisfy me, but it is what I have. If you experience road confusion, stop, rest, check the CCC radio, and proceed in daylight.

FINAL NOTE
The buffer zone people do not need us to survive. They have been not-needing-us for two hundred years. We are passing through something they built. Behave accordingly.
